gaps: Swap the literal waveform-as-landscape metaphor for an idea specific to the device, such as what gets 'caught' in a recording, and show it with real material and light
Develop a typographic system: a chosen or custom face, real scale contrast and type that interacts with the terrain on purpose. Right now it is default serif text placed on top
Give each frame its own composition and camera (macro, scale shifts, a hard cut to the product in use) instead of one horizon layout repeated with different peaks

tells: Dense, layered simulation work: shattered and extruded ribbons, liquid glass eyewear forming from fluid, caustics and bubbles. These are hard technical problems and they are solved well
The product is translated into material: the glasses are rebuilt as translucent liquid with internal structure, which follows the 'evolution' line
Every frame uses a different scale and camera (explosive wide shot, hero product, macro of the frame, cellular close-up), which implies real choreography
Real light: rim lighting, refraction and depth-of-field are consistent across the shots
Weaknesses: the type is a standard tech grotesk with a tracked-caps 'EVOLUTION' on top, and the single electric-blue palette is a common category convention
gaps: The typography is the weak point. The tracked-caps 'EVOLUTION' and the plain wordmark could be in any tech launch, so it needs type with a point of view that is integrated into the fluid
The all-blue palette is a category default. A second colour or a temperature shift would give it a recognisable identity, as C's red and gold does
Push the narrative beyond 'tech material forms from liquid' so the piece has a more specific idea that a viewer would remember

tells: A deliberate, unusual palette of cinnabar red, ivory, travertine and brushed gold, tied to a seasonal or lunar-new-year luxury story without falling into cliché
Very precise material work: matte stone plinths, gold inlay lines, a watch-movement gear train set inside a turntable, and soft but directional daylight with real contact shadows
The set design is built around the product's own geometry. The circles, arcs and ribbon loops echo the speaker's form and the fan-like ridges
Every frame is a well-composed poster, and the shots vary: a group still life, ribbons orbiting a macro detail, a top-down mechanism reveal, a hero shot and a final group
There is no visible headline type apart from the product logo. The absence mostly serves the piece because the brand is carried by the objects themselves
gaps: The motion implied is mostly elegant camera moves around a set. More surprise in the choreography (a transformation or reveal beyond the gear-movement shot) would make it memorable
The concept is luxury still life with seasonal colours. A sharper conceptual hook would take it from excellent craft to a piece people share
If type appears, it should match the material language, for example an engraved or gold-inlay end card, rather than relying on the product logo alone

tells: A real comedic idea runs through it: an 'I.O.U.' note left in place of the food you took, which turns into gifting and paying people back (coffee, beer, money, heart, gift icons). It is a specific, human insight, not a feature diagram
It mixes several aspect ratios and illustration styles (night-time van scene, stylised CG fridge, flat golf character, 3D emoji icons), which suggests a deliberate multi-spot social campaign
The golfer's three-pose sequence has clear timing and comedy, and the fridge reveal uses lighting and reflection to make the punchline land
Weaknesses: the styles are inconsistent from frame to frame, the icon grid is close to stock emoji, and the flat vector golfer comes near clip-art territory
gaps: Unify the visual language. The jump between CG fridge, flat vector character and emoji grid reads as a set of assets rather than one authored film
Raise the material and light craft of the flat and icon sections to the fridge shot's level, giving them texture, shadow and grounding
Bring hand-drawn or custom type beyond the 'I.O.U.' note into the system, for example as an end line, so the joke carries through to the brand moment

defects: Opening frame has a hard horizontal seam where the ripple and reflection plate meets the ridge plate. It reads as a compositing split, not a designed wipe.
In the reveal shot the ridge cuts through the 'Tern' wordmark and clips the 'n'. It reads as a layering accident, not a deliberate occlusion.
The final lockup peak touches the period of 'Lift to record.' The tangency looks unplanned.
Pairs show near-identical frames 1/6 s apart: slow linear camera drift, with ridges barely changing. 8 of 19 seconds are effectively static.
Shots cut on a rigid 2.5 s grid (2.5 / 5.0 / 7.5 / 10 / 12.5 s), visible as rectangular blocks in the spectrogram. The edit is metronomic, not phrased.
Device close-up is a flat, low-detail render: soft bevel, generic concentric-ring mics, and a gradient sheen with no real specular response.
The audio is rectangular full-band noise slabs (2.5–5 s, 10–12.5 s) with hard on/off edges, plus static harmonic stacks. It sounds like a generated synth bed, not mixed sound design.
The 'Caught whole.' spike is a stiff vertical extrusion with no anticipation or settle visible in the samples.
gaps: Motion: the waveform-to-landscape idea never gets a hero move. Ridges need to grow, crest and settle with real easing, overlap and follow-through. The camera drifts linearly and the transitions are hard cuts on a fixed grid, with no match cuts or handoffs between waveform, ripple and device.

Sound: replace the block-noise slabs with designed foley and room tone (wind, a recorder click, the tern call 'caught whole'). Build a real dynamic arc with a peak around 70% and a clean release, and land the transients on picture events, not on the 2.5 s timer.

Finish and composition: fix the plate seam and the accidental type occlusion. Render the device with proper materials and light. Give each shot a poster-grade focal point instead of empty sky or a half-cropped object, so the type-landscape interplay looks authored.
